About Gringo's Washboard Band

It started as a dare. In 2016, Zé "Gringo" Tábuas borrowed his grandmother's washboard, a box of sewing thimbles and a street corner in downtown Lisbon — and refused to leave until somebody danced. Somebody did. Then a banjo player joined, then a bass made from a washtub and a broomstick, and Gringo's Washboard Band was born.

“We play the music people made when they couldn't afford instruments. That's the whole idea — joy is cheap, but it takes work.”

Inspired by the jug bands of Memphis, the hokum of 1920s Chicago and the hot swing of Parisian cafés, the five musicians have spent a decade turning bars, festivals and, now and then, a laundromat into dance halls. The shows are loud, sweaty and impossible to watch sitting down.

Rub-a-Dub Blues, their third studio album, was recorded live to tape over four days in an old cork factory near Seixal. Twelve songs — eight originals and four lovingly mistreated standards — capture the band the way it sounds on a Saturday night: a little out of breath and grinning ear to ear.

"We tried overdubs once," laughs banjo player Rita Banjo. "It sounded like a band. We wanted it to sound like a party."

The band has toured Portugal, Spain, France and the Netherlands, shared stages with swing orchestras and punk bands alike, and once played a wedding aboard a moving tram. It is still looking for a room that can handle it.
